title: Frederick and Catherine
paragraphs: There was once a man named Frederick, who had a wife called Catherine, and the two had only recently married. One day Frederick said, “Kate, I’m off to work in the fields. I’ll be hungry when I get back, so have something tasty cooked for me, and a good mug of ale.” “All right,” she said, “it’ll all be ready.” When dinner time was getting close, Catherine took a nice steak, the only meat she had in the house, and set it on the fire to fry. Soon the steak was turning brown and sizzling in the pan, and Catherine stood over it with a fork, turning it. Then she said to herself, “The steak is nearly done. I might as well fetch the ale from the cellar.” So she left the pan on the fire, picked up a big jug, went down to the cellar and tapped the ale cask. The beer poured into the jug while Catherine stood and watched. Then suddenly a thought struck her: “I never shut the dog in. He could be making off with the steak. Good thing I remembered!” So she dashed up the cellar steps, and sure enough, the thieving cur had the steak in his mouth and was trotting away with it.

Catherine tore off after him, and the dog tore off across the field, but he was faster than she was and kept a firm hold on the steak. “Well, it’s gone, and ‘what can’t be cured must be endured,’” said Catherine. She turned around, and since she had run a long way and was worn out, she strolled home slowly to cool off.

All this while the ale had been running too, because Catherine had not turned off the tap. When the jug was full, the beer spilled over onto the floor and kept going until the cask was empty. When she reached the cellar stairs, she saw what had happened. “Good heavens!” she said. “How am I going to hide this mess from Frederick?” She thought for a while, and finally remembered the sack of fine flour they had bought at the last fair. If she sprinkled that over the floor, it would soak up the ale nicely. “How lucky that we kept that flour,” she said. “Now it’s useful.” Off she went to fetch it, but she set it down right on top of the big jug of beer and knocked it over, so that all the ale she had saved went swimming across the floor as well. “Ah well,” she said, “if one goes, the other might as well follow.” Then she scattered the flour all over the cellar, delighted with her own cleverness, and said, “Doesn’t it look neat and clean!”

At noon Frederick came home. “Well, wife,” he called, “what’s for dinner?” “Oh, Frederick,” she answered, “I was frying you a steak, but while I went down to draw the ale, the dog ran off with it. While I was chasing him, the ale ran out, and when I tried to dry up the ale with the sack of flour we got at the fair, I knocked over the jug. But the cellar is nice and dry now, and it looks so clean!” “Kate, Kate,” he said, “how could you do all this? Why did you leave the steak frying and the ale running, and then ruin all the flour?” “Well, Frederick,” she said, “I didn’t know it was wrong. You should have told me before.”

The husband thought to himself, “If my wife runs things like this, I’d better keep a sharp eye out.” Now he had a good deal of gold in the house, so he said to Catherine, “What pretty yellow buttons these are! I’ll put them in a box and bury them in the garden. But mind you never go near them or touch them.” “No, Frederick,” she said, “I never will.” As soon as he had gone, some peddlers came by with earthenware plates and dishes and asked whether she wanted to buy any. “Oh dear, I’d love to buy some, but I have no money. If you had any use for yellow buttons, we might do business.” “Yellow buttons!” they said. “Let’s have a look at them.” “Go into the garden and dig where I tell you, and you’ll find the yellow buttons. I don’t dare go myself.” So the rogues went, and when they saw what these yellow buttons really were, they carried them all off and left her plenty of plates and dishes. She arranged them all around the house for show, and when Frederick came back, he cried, “Kate, what have you done?” “Look,” she said, “I bought all this with your yellow buttons. But I didn’t touch them myself. The peddlers went and dug them up on their own.” “Wife, wife,” said Frederick, “what a fine mess you’ve made! Those yellow buttons were all the money we had. How could you do such a thing?” “Well,” she answered, “I didn’t know there was any harm in it. You should have told me.”

Catherine stood thinking for a while, and then said to her husband, “Listen, Frederick, we’ll soon get the gold back. Let’s run after the thieves.” “All right, we’ll try,” he answered. “But take some butter and cheese with you, so we have something to eat on the way.” “Very well,” she said, and they set out. Frederick walked faster, and he left his wife some way behind. “It doesn’t matter,” she thought. “When we turn back, I’ll be that much closer to home than he is.”

Soon she came to the top of a hill. A road ran down its side, so narrow that the cart wheels always scraped the trees on either side as they went by. “Oh, look,” she said, “how they’ve bruised and hurt those poor trees. They’ll never heal.” She felt sorry for them, so she used the butter to grease every one of them, so the wheels wouldn’t hurt them so much. While she was busy with this kindly work, one of her cheeses dropped out of the basket and rolled down the hill. Catherine looked but couldn’t see where it had gone, so she said, “Well, I suppose the other one will go the same way and find you. It has younger legs than I do.” Then she rolled the other cheese after it, and off it went, nobody knows where, down the hill. But she said she supposed they knew the way and would follow her, and she couldn’t stand there all day waiting for them.

At last she caught up with Frederick, who asked her for something to eat. She gave him the dry bread. “Where are the butter and cheese?” he said. “Oh,” she answered, “I used the butter to grease those poor trees the wheels were scraping. And one of the cheeses ran away, so I sent the other after it to find it. I expect they’re both somewhere on the road together.” “What a goose you are, doing such silly things!” said her husband. “How can you say that?” she said. “I’m sure you never told me not to.”

They ate the dry bread together, and Frederick said, “Kate, I hope you locked the door properly when you left.” “No,” she answered, “you didn’t tell me to.” “Then go home and do it now, before we go any farther,” said Frederick, “and bring something to eat with you.”

Catherine did as he said, and on the way she thought to herself, “Frederick wants something to eat, but I don’t think he cares much for butter and cheese. I’ll bring him a bag of good nuts and the vinegar, since I’ve often seen him take some.”

When she got home, she bolted the back door, but the front door she lifted off its hinges, saying, “Frederick told me to lock the door, but surely it can’t be safer anywhere than with me.” So she took her time on the way back, and when she caught up with her husband she called out, “There you are, Frederick, there’s the door itself. You can guard it as carefully as you like.” “Good grief!” he said. “What a clever wife I have! I sent you to make the house secure, and you take the door away, so anyone can walk in and out as they please. Still, since you brought the door, you can carry it around with you for your trouble.” “Very well,” she answered, “I’ll carry the door, but I won’t carry the nuts and the vinegar bottle too. That would be too heavy a load. So if you don’t mind, I’ll tie them to the door.”

Frederick naturally had no objection to that, and they went into the wood to look for the thieves, but they couldn’t find them. When it got dark, they climbed a tree to spend the night. They had barely settled when who should come along but the very rogues they were hunting. They were real scoundrels, the kind of people who find things before they’re lost. They were tired, so they sat down and lit a fire right under the tree where Frederick and Catherine were. Frederick slid down the other side and picked up some stones. Then he climbed back up and tried to hit the thieves on the head with them, but all they said was, “It must be nearly morning, the wind’s knocking the fir cones down.”

Catherine, with the door on her shoulder, was getting very tired, but she thought it was the nuts on it that made it so heavy. So she said quietly, “Frederick, I’ll have to let the nuts go.” “No,” he answered, “not now, they’ll find us out.” “I can’t help it, they’ve got to go.” “Oh, all right, then hurry up and throw them down, if you must.” Away the nuts rattled down through the branches, and one of the thieves cried, “Good Lord, it’s hailing!”

A little while later, Catherine felt the door was still very heavy, so she whispered to Frederick, “I’ll have to pour the vinegar out.” “Please don’t,” he answered, “it will give us away.” “I can’t help it,” she said, “it has to go.” So she poured all the vinegar down, and the thieves said, “What a heavy dew there is!”

At last it dawned on Catherine that it was the door itself that had been so heavy all along. So she whispered, “Frederick, I’ll have to throw the door down soon.” But he begged and pleaded with her not to, sure that it would betray them. “Here it goes, anyway,” she said, and down went the door onto the thieves with such a crash that they screamed “Murder!” and, not knowing what was falling on them, ran off as fast as they could and left all the gold behind. So when Frederick and Catherine climbed down, they found all their money there, safe and sound.
